questions.q: How does Howard Okonjo answer the director's question about whether a third disagreeing system might exist?
options: By guaranteeing with certainty that no third system could ever disagree
By refusing to answer the question as out of scope for a board meeting
By honestly stating that a negative can't be proven, but describing the standing dual-check layer and a new 30-day sweep as the real, repeatable process for catching the next one
By blaming the compliance team for not checking a third system already
questions.explain: Howard's credible answer names a specific process rather than claiming false certainty — the honest claim is a repeatable chance of catching the next gap, not that no gap could ever exist.

questions.q: How does Mara Voss reframe the question 'why did it take a script to catch what an audit should have caught'?
options: By agreeing the audit was broken and apologizing on Renee Castellano's behalf

By explaining that the audit was scoped to the common case (group-based access) and the automation was built specifically for the uncommon case (direct grants) — two methods with different scopes, used together on purpose
By claiming the script replaces the need for any future compliance audits
By insisting the question is unfair and should not have been asked
questions.explain: Mara reframes the premise honestly without dodging it — the audit wasn't broken, it simply had a different, narrower scope than the automation was designed to cover.

questions.q: What makes both of this lesson's board answers credible rather than evasive?
options: They both promise the exact same incident can never happen again
They both describe a specific, checkable process and are honest about exactly where confidence runs out, rather than claiming unearned certainty
They both avoid giving the board any concrete detail at all
They both shift responsibility onto a third party not in the room
questions.explain: A board can tell the difference between 'trust us, it's handled' and a specific account of what was built and what it does and doesn't guarantee — the second kind of answer survives follow-up questions.

questions.q: What is the general principle this lesson teaches about answering a hard security question from a non-technical stakeholder?
options: Always claim full certainty to reassure the stakeholder, regardless of what's actually known
Avoid answering directly and redirect to a written report instead
Show the process that justifies real, specific confidence, and be honest about where that confidence actually ends
Only answer questions asked by the most senior person in the room
questions.explain: Defensiveness or false certainty reads as evasion even when the underlying work is solid; naming the real boundary of what's known reads as competence.

questions.q: Why is 'we fixed it' not, by itself, a sufficient answer to either hard question in this lesson?
options: Because the fix described in Lesson 19 was never actually completed
Because it doesn't address whether a similar or different gap could exist elsewhere, or why the original method missed this one — the real questions being asked
Because board members do not care whether something was fixed
Because 'we fixed it' is technically inaccurate in this case
questions.explain: Both director questions are forward-looking and process-focused, not just asking whether this specific incident was resolved, so 'we fixed it' alone doesn't actually answer what's being asked.
